items.title: Black Feminist Thought

items.author: Patricia Hill Collins
parts: Ch. 11 Black Feminist Epistemology (pp. 251–271) · in progress
Ch. 4 Mammies, Matriarchs, and Other Controlling Images · to read
items.question: What standards decide whose knowledge counts, and what alternative epistemology do U.S. Black women use to validate knowledge?
argument: Knowledge validation in the U.S. is controlled by elite White men, so Black women's knowledge is excluded both institutionally and epistemologically (positivism as the example).
Black women draw on an alternative epistemology with four dimensions: lived experience, dialogue, ethic of caring, ethic of personal accountability.
Black feminist thought is partial, situated knowledge; partiality, not universality, is the condition of being heard, and alternative epistemologies challenge the process of validating truth itself.
concepts: subjugated knowledge: knowledge suppressed within dominant institutions
knowledge validation processes: institutions + Eurocentric epistemologies that legitimate knowledge
lived experience as a criterion of meaning: those who lived an experience are more credible (knowledge vs. wisdom)
dialogue: claims tested in community, not adversarial debate (call-and-response)
ethic of caring: individual uniqueness, emotion, empathy
ethic of personal accountability: claims assessed with the speaker's character and values
outsider-within: Black women in the academy moving between interpretive communities
structure: Black women as agents of knowledge (3 groups)
Method: theoretical argument + Black women's voices, literature, interviews

items.title: Tracking Epistemic Violence, Tracking Practices of Silencing
items.author: Kristie Dotson
items.subject: final-paper
items.question: How can we identify and distinguish practices of silencing that members of oppressed groups face when they testify? (p. 236)
argument: Dotson defines epistemic violence as an audience's failure to communicatively reciprocate, owing to pernicious ignorance.

Using this definition, she distinguishes two practices of silencing: testimonial quieting (the audience fails to recognize the speaker as a knower) and testimonial smothering (the speaker cuts short her own risky testimony).
Because silencing is located in the audience's failure, the burden of proof shifts away from the silenced speaker.
concepts: epistemic violence: an audience's failure to communicatively reciprocate, intentionally or not, owing to pernicious ignorance
pernicious ignorance: reliable ignorance that, in a given context, causes harm
reliable ignorance: counterfactual incompetence; consistently failing to track the truth in some domain
testimonial quieting: an audience fails to identify a speaker as a knower
testimonial smothering: a speaker truncates her own testimony to what the audience demonstrates competence for (coerced self-silencing)
testimonial competence: the speaker's judgment that an audience has shown it can find her testimony accurately intelligible
situated ignorance: ignorance that follows from one's social position or epistemic location
structure: Hornsby's reciprocity → speakers depend on audiences
Define epistemic violence + answer 3 objections (incl. the 3-year-old case)
Conclusion: dispersing the burden of proof
quotes: "Epistemic violence does not require intention, nor does it require capacity." (p. 240)
mine: Evidence that the harm of hate speech does not end at the moment of utterance but produces later silencing (smothering).
Shifts the focus from speaker to audience → educational question: a classroom (as audience) must demonstrate testimonial competence to students who have been hurt, and refuse uptake to hate speech.
Smothering → experiences go unspoken → gaps in hermeneutical resources: support for the vicious cycle of testimonial and hermeneutical injustice.
questions: If we all see from distorted positions, who can judge an audience's ignorance to be "pernicious," and from what position? (cf. pp. 241, 243 vs. 248)
What harms of silencing escape a framework built on testimony and truth?
If harm is context-dependent, what criteria can identify it without inflating the concept or flattening context?
Is the norm of reciprocity itself an idealization?
Three-year-old case: must the harm of epistemic violence fall on the speaker, or does any bad outcome count?
related: Fricker (2007): testimonial injustice. The hearer judges the speaker's credibility; in Dotson, the speaker judges the hearer's competence (the opposite direction).
Langton (1993): locutionary silencing; compare with smothering (n. 12).
Butler (1997): speech forms the subject → grounds for my critique (the reciprocity norm as an idealization).
